notes:
I found sources for most verses, but not all. Verses 23–24, 27–28 and 38–39 are missing because I ran out of searches and page reads. The pages I opened in full (Enduring Word, Precept Austin, bible.org) cut off before verse 23, so most of these notes come from short search-result excerpts of those and other commentary pages.

**The main split, in brief:** Almost everyone reads vv. 23–35 as Antiochus IV Epiphanes. The big disagreement starts at v. 36: is "the king" still Antiochus, or someone later?

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 25:** Matthew Henry says Antiochus musters his strength and courage against Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, who comes out to meet him with a very large army. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-29.html

**v. 26:** Henry says Egypt's king is betrayed by his own advisers, the men that eat of his bread and live upon him, being bribed by Antiochus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html
Bob Utley says the verse seems to refer to the political intrigue occurring in the Egyptian court. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11

**v. 29:** Precept Austin says Antiochus was angered when Ptolemy VI and his brother made up, so he invaded Egypt a second time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary2
Utley says this second campaign is recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:29 and Polybius. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11

**v. 30:**
- **Who the "ships of Kittim" are.** Barnes says "Kittim" properly means Cyprus. Over time it came to mean the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean, especially Greece. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-30.htm
- **What happened.** Barnes and Gill say Rome sent envoys led by Popilius Laenas, who ordered Antiochus out of Egypt. Popilius drew a circle in the sand around him and demanded an answer before he stepped out. Antiochus gave in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-30.htm
- **His anger turned on Jerusalem.** Polybius, cited by Barnes, says he left Egypt furious, and he took that anger out on Jerusalem and the Jews. Matthew Poole and the Geneva Bible notes say Jewish apostates encouraged him: first Jason the high priest, then Menelaus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-30.htm
- **Later uses.** The Bible Hub study notes say this rampage foreshadows end-time hostility to God's people (Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2). https://biblehub.com/daniel/11-30.htm

**v. 31:**
- Benson explains the "abomination" as the idol Antiochus put on the altar of burnt offering, probably Jupiter (Zeus). It is called the abomination "that maketh desolate" because it drove true worship and worshippers out of the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-31.htm
- Utley says Antiochus ordered a pig offered on the altar and set up a shrine to Zeus in the Holy Place, citing 1 Maccabees 1:54, 59. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11
- The Bible Hub notes point out that Jesus treats the abomination as still future (Matthew 24:15). https://biblehub.com/daniel/11-31.htm
- Thomas Ice says the phrase means the same thing in all three places it appears in Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/ice_thomas/Mat24-25/Mat24-25_Part13.cfm

**v. 32:**
- **"Corrupt."** Ellicott says the word literally means "make profane." These apostates started out indifferent to true religion and ended up hostile to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-32.htm
- **"Flattery."** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say this means promises of favour.
- **"The people who know their God."** JFB identify them as the Maccabees and their followers. Benson's application: while others give in to the tyrant, they stand their ground and make him ashamed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-32.htm
- Chuck Smith links them to Judas Maccabeus retaking and rededicating the temple, which Hanukkah celebrates. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-35.html

**vv. 33–35:** Gill says the wise "fall" not into sin or false teaching, but into suffering because they stay loyal to God's word and worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-35.html
On v. 35, Guzik says the terror could last only as long as God had set, and God had a purpose even in the persecution. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Dan/Dan_11.cfm

**v. 36: the turning point.** The main readings are listed under Part 2 below. Two more points:
- The Bible Hub article says Hippolytus identified this king as the end-time Antichrist, separate from Antiochus, and that Tertullian and Irenaeus agreed. https://biblehub.com/q/Daniel_11_36_and_Antichrist_prophecy.htm
- Precept Austin argues from the pronouns: the "him" whom the king of the South attacks in v. 40 is the v. 36 king, so he can't be Antiochus, the king of the North. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary2

**v. 37: "the one desired by women."** Readings:
1. **The Messiah.** Many futurists say every godly Jewish woman hoped to bear the Messiah. Constable takes this view, and J. Vernon McGee follows it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-37.html
2. **A goddess or god worshipped by women.** Options include Tammuz/Adonis (Cambridge Bible) and Nanaea, whose temple Antiochus died trying to plunder (Pulpit Commentary, which traces this view to Ephrem the Syrian and Jerome). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-37.htm
3. **Natural love or affection.** Keil & Delitzsch take it as the love of women, meaning he casts off all human tenderness. Ellicott argues that if it named a god, the next phrase, "nor for any other god," would make no sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-37.html
4. **Forbidding marriage.** See Gill and Clarke under Part 2.
5. **Homosexuality.** Gotquestions grants this is possible but says it is not the most plausible reading. https://www.gotquestions.org/antichrist-gay.html

**v. 40:**
- Guzik says the peoples named are hard to identify. The South may be Egypt or the Arab world. The North may be the Antichrist's realm or Russia. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Constable lists three views: the king of the North is the Antichrist (Archer, Young); a separate force (Pentecost, Leupold); or a minor ruler. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-40.html
- Against a purely future reading, Utley says the North/South labels tie the chapter to the Seleucid–Ptolemy rivalry. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11

**vv. 41–43:** The Light of Israel commentary says that, like Antiochus, the Antichrist will still attack Israel despite his other troubles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-45.html
Chuck Smith sees him as leader of a united Europe pushing into Africa: Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia. Same page.

**v. 44:**
- Smith says the alarming news is troops from China and Russia. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-45.html
- Barnes, who keeps reading Antiochus, places this in his last campaign east: probably putting down a revolt in Armenia on the way to Persia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-45.htm

**v. 45:**
- **The place.** Ellicott takes "the seas" as the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. He notes the king dies in the same area other prophets name for the Antichrist's overthrow (Ezekiel 39, Joel 3, Zechariah 14). https://biblehub.com/daniel/11-45.htm
- **If it's Antiochus.** Cambridge says he actually died at Tabae in Persia. JFB connect his death to his grief at his army's defeat by the Jews and his failed temple raid in Elymais. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-45.htm
- **Henry's reading.** He says Antiochus set up his royal tent at Emmaus near Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-40.html
- **Futurist reading.** Constable says the Antichrist's headquarters will be in Jerusalem, and he will be defeated there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-45.html

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ (mainly vv. 36–45)

- **Reformed:**
  - Calvin says the king of v. 36 is neither Antiochus nor a leap ahead to Antichrist, but the Roman Empire, which he calls a perpetual series. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol25/htm/vi.xxxi.htm
  - On v. 37, Calvin mentions views that apply it to the Pope (enforced celibacy) or to Mohammed, then rejects both. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_daniel_volume_2/daniel_11_37.htm
  - Albert Barnes, a Presbyterian, holds that v. 36 still means Antiochus. He argues the text gives no sign of a change of subject. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html
  - Matthew Henry sees the text moving from Antiochus to Antichrist, and to Rome in its pagan, Christian and papal stages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-36.htm
- **Baptist:**
  - John Gill says the king is Rome, especially the papal Antichrist. He reads "desire of women" as the ban on priests marrying (1 Timothy 4:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-36.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/fre/dar/daniel/11-37.html
  - John MacArthur says the text jumps centuries between vv. 35 and 36 to the final Antichrist. He says interpreters who refer the verses to Antiochus do so because they refuse to accept predictive prophecy. https://www.gty.org/resources/study-guides/print/27-29/the-reign-of-rebellion-part-2
- **Methodist / Wesleyan:**
  - Wesley calls Antiochus an outstanding type of the Antichrist, but says the verses refer mainly to Antiochus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html
  - Benson takes the same line. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-36.htm
  - Adam Clarke applies v. 37 to Greek and Latin church rules against marriage, and v. 40 to the Turks. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-40.html
- **Lutheran:** Utley lists Luther among those who read vv. 36–45 as the papal system. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11
  Precept Austin quotes Luther saying the chapter refers to both Antiochus and Antichrist. It also quotes Calvin rebuking Luther for this. https://www.preceptaustin.org/last-eschatos
- **Anglican:** Ellicott says the northern king is still in view, but Antiochus's features gradually "fade" from the portrait, which comes to match Paul's Antichrist in 2 Thessalonians 2:4. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html
- **Pentecostal / charismatic** (Calvary Chapel; I found nothing on the Assemblies of God site): Guzik sees a shift to a "last days Antiochus Epiphanes." His reason is that Antiochus put up a statue of Zeus, not of himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
  Chuck Smith reads the "indignation" as the Great Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html

## Part 3: Other views

- **Modern scholarship:** I could not reach netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.
  - The Cambridge Bible (Driver) says it goes against all sound principles of exegesis to switch subjects partway through one continuous description. It reads vv. 36–39 as Antiochus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/11-36.htm
  - Utley (bible.org) says vv. 36–39 partly fit Antiochus and vv. 40–45 don't fit him at all. He suggests the vagueness may be deliberate, so the passage can apply to anyone who embodies human rebellion. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11
  - Guzik notes, and rejects, the critical view that the chapter is history written after the events. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- **Catholic / Orthodox:** I found nothing on newadvent, catholic.com or oca.org. Other commentators report two early Church views (not read directly):
  - Barnes says Jerome, among others, saw an Antichrist reference from v. 36 on. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/11-36.html
  - Utley says Jerome saw a double reference (Antiochus and Antichrist) running through vv. 21–45, and that Chrysostom started it at v. 1. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-11
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this passage.
